title: Night Shift
intro: Everybody rolls their quads. This one goes where tennis actually lands. Your feet. The deep calf that helps you brake. The inside of the thigh from wide balls and the outside from pushing off. The backs of your thighs from all the stopping. Then your mid back and chest from serving and overheads, and three minutes of slow breathing to finish. You need a roller and a ball, and a tennis ball is fine.

Slow is the whole technique. When you find a sore spot, stop on it and take three breaths. Don't saw back and forth. Aim for firm pressure. Rolling helps you feel better and move a bit easier for a while, and that's genuinely it. It doesn't clear anything out of your muscles and it doesn't break anything up. So do it because the day is over and you want to feel human.

before.label: Never roll
before.text: Your lower back, the front or side of your neck, the back of your knee, the inside of your elbow, your armpit or right into the groin crease. Nothing that's swollen, hot, bruised or freshly hurt.

before.label: Leave that spot alone
before.text: If something grabbed during play and it's still sore now, leave it alone and get it looked at. If it's sharp, or you get pins and needles, back off.

before.label: Swollen calf
before.text: If one calf is swollen, warm or tender and you didn't strain it playing, don't roll it and see a doctor the same day.

exercises.name: Soleus Roll
exercises.note: If your calf is still sore from playing, skip this one.

exercises.name: Adductor Roll
exercises.note: If a groin is still sore from playing, skip this one.

exercises.name: Extended Exhale Breathing
exercises.note: In 4, out 8. If you feel dizzy or tingly, go back to normal breathing.

good: Lie on your back with one hand on your belly and let each breath out slowly empty it
Feel that hand rise and fall while your chest stays quiet
